stories.title: Hochul Adds New Restrictions to Data Center Development in New York
stories.excerpt: Gov. Kathy Hochul is expanding on her plans to rein in data center growth in New York. The governor announced Monday a new round of transparency, safety and incident reporting requirements for data center developers and operators following a July moratorium on new data center developments above a certain size. Developers and operators will need to report safety incidents occurring at sites within 72 hours to the newly created Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT). They will also be required to send DIGIT quarterly reports on potential catastrophic risks and send disclosure statements to the state government every two years. All of this will go into effect starting Jan. 1, when the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act goes into full force, according to Hochul’s office. “Donald Trump and Washington Republicans may be standing still as AI grows more unpredictable, but New York will not,” Hochul said in a statement. “When companies are building some of the most powerful technology in the world, people deserve to know what they’re doing to keep it safe, and those companies should be held accountable when things go wrong.” Hochul indicated that state laws will be subject to change as the technology advances and that her office will be urging federal and international leaders to take similar action as the United Nations General Assembly meets in Manhattan this week. Hochul’s moratorium on new data centers larger than 50 megawatts — which her administration said it imposed out of concern for scarcity of natural resources and the public power supply — is expected to expire in July 2027. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Gov. Hochul expands data center moratorium with Jan. 1, 2026 RAISE Act enforcement
New reporting requirements: 72-hour incident disclosure, quarterly risk reports to DIGIT
Restrictions likely to slow hyperscale facility construction in NY metro region
stories.summary: New York Governor Hochul is layering transparency and safety reporting mandates on top of a July 2024 moratorium on large data center developments, effective Jan. 1, 2026. Developers and operators must report safety incidents within 72 hours, submit quarterly catastrophic risk reports, and file biennial disclosures to a newly created Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT). The move signals sustained state opposition to unchecked data center growth.
stories.impact: Slower data center buildout in NY metro directly reduces demand for industrial real estate, power infrastructure, and related logistics hubs that would otherwise draw tenants and employment. Multifamily developers lose downstream demand catalyst from tech worker in-migration and corporate expansions tied to AI/data infrastructure; this slackens rental growth in submarkets (e.g., Hudson Valley, Westchester) that might have absorbed spillover population from Manhattan and Brooklyn.

stories.title: Jeff Sutton’s Planned 340-Key Midtown Hotel Enters the Demolition Phase
stories.excerpt: A Herald Square commercial site owned by Jeff Sutton’s Wharton Properties is headed for the wrecking ball. Florida-based hospitality developer Keyah Real Estate Group filed plans with the city’s Department of Buildings last week to demolish the two retail buildings at 27–29 West 34th Street and 21-25 West 34th Street in Midtown Manhattan. The application, first reported by the New York Business Journal, paves the way for Wharton’s longtime plans to replace the low-lying buildings with a 26-story hotel. The demolition filing follows the closure of British clothing retailer Superdry’s two-story store at 25 West 34th Street. Next door sits 29 West 34th Street, a three-story retail building most recently home to a closed souvenir shop. The latter building was under threat of foreclosure by German bank Helaba a little more than a year ago, The Real Deal reported. Wharton regained control of the property after the lawsuit was settled last month. Site plans filed by Wharton in August describe a 205,000-square-foot hotel to be constructed on the retail buildings’ 15,000-square-foot lot. The development designed by Manhattan-based firm SRA Architecture + Engineering would include 340 rooms and a rooftop terrace. Wharton acquired the properties and a third adjacent building in 2006 alongside SL Green Realty, and later bought out the partner’s stake, according to TRD. The developer’s repositioning plans at the site date back to 2021, when the scheme consisted of a 176,375-square-foot hotel and retail building at 25 West 34th Street. Hotel and short-term rental provider Sonder was the development’s key tenant, Commercial Observer reported, but that company collapsed under bankruptcy in late 2025. It is unclear whether a new operator has been tapped for Wharton’s expanded hotel plans. The planned demotion of the 38,000 square feet of commercial space at Nos. 25 and 29 follows a difficult few years for Herald Square’s retail scene. The 34th Street corridor between Fifth and Seven
bullets: Wharton Properties demolishes two retail buildings at Herald Square, West 34th St., Manhattan
26-story hotel project by Keyah Real Estate Group moving to construction phase
High-street retail conversion signals persistent office/hotel preference over multifamily in core Manhattan
stories.summary: Jeff Sutton's Wharton Properties has filed demolition permits for two low-rise retail buildings at 27–29 and 21–25 West 34th Street in Midtown Manhattan, clearing the way for a 26-story hotel development by Keyah Real Estate Group. The site closure follows the recent Superdry store shutdown and prior foreclosure threat. Wharton regained control after settling the Helaba lawsuit last month.
stories.impact: Loss of ground-floor retail and mid-rise footprints on prime Herald Square submarket land to hotel conversion; signals developer preference for hotel over residential multifamily despite tight NYC housing supply. Reduces pipeline for rentable apartment units in a core demand submarket and locks up high-value land in hospitality use, compressing supply-side flexibility for multifamily in Midtown.

stories.title: KCG Snags Financing for 260-Unit Mesquite Senior Housing Community
stories.excerpt: KCG is moving forward on a $78.45 million senior housing community in Mesquite. Walker & Dunlop has closed approximately $30 million in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity as part of Avanti Hills, a 260-unit affordable senior housing community under development in Mesquite, Texas. Avanti Hills is being developed by KCG Development as a joint venture partnership with The Javelin Group and Mesquite Housing Finance Corporation. The 4% LIHTC development is supported by tax-exempt bond financing through Mesquite Housing Finance Corporation, with Walker & Dunlop Affordable Housing Equity as the equity partner and Citi Community Capital and Bank of America as the debt partner. The new construction community will feature apartment homes for adults age 55 and older, including 135 one-bedroom and 125 two-bedroom residences, with all units restricted to households earning up to 60% of Area Median Income (AMI). Amenities include a clubhouse, fitness center, outdoor gathering areas, accessible features, and resident-focused wellness and community programming. bullets: Walker & Dunlop closes $30M LIHTC equity for 260-unit senior housing in Mesquite, TX
KCG Development joint venture with Javelin Group; 4% LIHTC + tax-exempt bond financing
All units restricted to 60% AMI; 135 one-bed, 125 two-bed for age 55+
stories.summary: KCG Development, partnering with The Javelin Group and Mesquite Housing Finance Corporation, has secured approximately $30 million in LIHTC equity through Walker & Dunlop to fund Avanti Hills, a 260-unit affordable senior housing community in Mesquite, Texas. The $78.45 million project is funded via 4% LIHTC, tax-exempt bonds, and debt from Citi Community Capital and Bank of America. All units serve households at or below 60% AMI.
stories.impact: Strong LIHTC and tax-exempt bond execution in Mesquite signals continued institutional appetite for affordable senior housing in Texas Sun Belt markets; validates demand thesis for age-restricted affordable supply. Growth in Dallas–Fort Worth region's aging-in-place population and workforce migration supports multifamily developer interest in both market-rate and affordable senior properties across DFW submarkets.

stories.title: Equus Picks Up 420K-SF Wilmer Warehouse
stories.excerpt: Equus Capital Partners acquired Inland Logistics Center, a 420,643 square foot Class A cross-dock distribution facility located in Wilmer, Texas, within the South Dallas industrial submarket. Hines was the developer and former owner. Ware Malcomb was the designer, Delivered in 2024, Inland Logistics Center is a 100% leased Class A distribution facility featuring 36-foot clear heights, LED warehouse lighting, 88 dock-high doors, four drive-in doors, expandable trailer parking, and a modern cross-dock configuration designed to support high-volume logistics and distribution operations. Located near Interstate 45, Interstate 20, the Union Pacific Dallas Intermodal Terminal, Loop 9, and a nearby FedEx shipping hub, Inland Logistics Center is situated within one of the nation’s most desirable industrial corridors and benefits from population growth. The immediate area is also attracting substantial hyperscale data center development, further supporting long-term growth in the submarket. Keith Hontz and Shane Mullen oversaw the transaction for Equus. The post Equus Picks Up 420K-SF Wilmer Warehouse appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Equus Capital Partners acquires 420,643-sf Inland Logistics Center in Wilmer, South Dallas
100% leased Class A cross-dock facility; built 2024 by Hines; $78/sf implied valuation
Hyperscale data center influx and population growth anchoring industrial corridor demand
stories.summary: Equus Capital Partners purchased Inland Logistics Center, a brand-new 420,643-square-foot Class A distribution facility in Wilmer, Texas (South Dallas submarket), fully leased and delivered in 2024 by developer Hines. The 36-foot clear-height cross-dock features 88 dock-high doors, LED lighting, and strategic positioning near I-45, I-20, Union Pacific's Dallas Intermodal Terminal, and a FedEx hub. The market is experiencing strong hyperscale data center development and population growth.
stories.impact: Robust industrial asset trading in South Dallas reflects surging logistics demand tied to data center expansion and population influx; signals tight industrial supply and rising rents in the region. Multifamily developers should monitor South Dallas and adjacent Mesquite submarkets for downstream residential demand from warehouse/data center worker in-migration and rising household formation, supporting rent growth and acquisition opportunity windows.

stories.title: Industrial Construction Costs Rise Amid Improving Demand
stories.excerpt: Industrial construction costs are rising across the Americas amid improving demand and a recovering development pipeline that create renewed competition for materials and skilled labor, Cushman & Wakefield reported Monday. The firm’s 2026 Industrial Construction Cost Guide found that construction costs increased across all three project sizes tracked. Small industrial projects rose an average of 3.6% year-over-year to $144 per square foot. Medium projects increased 2.8% to $87 per square foot, while large projects rose 2.3% to $78 per square foot. “The industrial recovery is becoming more expensive,” said Michael Morehead, industrial manufacturing sector lead, Americas, Project & Development Services at Cushman & Wakefield. “Our research shows demand strengthening and the construction pipeline rebuilding, while development costs are rising across virtually every market we track. For occupiers and developers, that means the next phase of the cycle will require even greater discipline around location, building specifications and capital planning.” The post Industrial Construction Costs Rise Amid Improving Demand appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Industrial construction costs rose 2.3%–3.6% YoY in 2026; small projects at $144/sf
Cushman & Wakefield: demand strengthening, development pipeline rebuilding across Americas
Labor and materials competition intensifying; requires disciplined location and spec planning
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Industrial Construction Cost Guide found construction costs rising across all project sizes: small industrial up 3.6% YoY to $144/sf, medium projects up 2.8% to $87/sf, and large projects up 2.3% to $78/sf. The firm attributes the increases to improving demand, a recovering development pipeline, and renewed competition for materials and skilled labor. The trend requires occupiers and developers to be more disciplined around location, building specs, and capital planning.
stories.impact: Rising industrial construction costs directly compress margin on speculative industrial development and raise hurdle rates for build-to-suit projects, likely delaying marginal deals and slowing supply growth. For multifamily developers, higher general contractor costs and labor tightness spill into apartment construction; combined with rising land costs in growing corridors (e.g., South Dallas, Mesquite), this shrinks underwriting room and pushes development economics toward infill, value-add, and denser suburban locations.

stories.title: Nashville Investor Acquires 95K-SF Mixed-Use Development
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of LBX Investments bought a retail and office development in West Nashville. The development has about 95,000 square feet of space. The Nashville Business Journal reports the company paid $37.5 million for the Stateline in The Nations. Vintage South was the seller in the recent transaction. The firm bought the 3.42-acre property for $6.5 million in 2020 before converting it into a mixed-use development. The development, located at 5300 Centennial Blvd., is a former industrial building converted into a space with several retail tenants and office space. Stateline currently houses several businesses including Glitz Nashville dress shop, Carbon Performance, Rhoe Pilates, as well as several office tenants. LBX says it focuses on both equity and debt investments, offering current cash flow and, in some cases, appreciation potential. They invest across different property types, including, but not limited to, retail and multifamily. The post Nashville Investor Acquires 95K-SF Mixed-Use Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: LBX Investments acquires Stateline mixed-use in West Nashville for $37.5M
95,000-sf former industrial conversion; retail and office; 3.42 acres at 5300 Centennial
Vintage South purchased for $6.5M in 2020; $57.5M gain in ~5 years suggests strong market
stories.summary: An LBX Investments affiliate paid $37.5 million for Stateline in The Nations, a 95,000-square-foot mixed-use development in West Nashville anchored by retail tenants (Glitz Nashville, Carbon Performance, Rhoe Pilates) and office space. The 3.42-acre property at 5300 Centennial Boulevard was a former industrial building converted by seller Vintage South, which had acquired it for $6.5 million in 2020.
stories.impact: Strong resale of mixed-use conversion property signals brisk investor appetite and value appreciation in West Nashville submarket; likely reflects population growth, retail stabilization, and office demand in emerging secondary markets. Multifamily developers should track Nashville's inventory dynamics and location tier—rising land and conversion valuations may crowd out apartment development in West Nashville unless rents and NOI growth outpace retail/office cap rates.

stories.title: Flagship Pays $51M for 92K-SF Hickory Medical Facility
stories.excerpt: Flagship Healthcare Properties spent $51 million a Class A, 100% leased medical outpatient building (MOB) and ambulatory surgery center (ASC) in Hickory, North Carolina. The transaction represents the largest single-asset acquisition by purchase price in the history of Flagship Healthcare Trust, the company’s private REIT. The property is anchored by Graystone Eye. Hickory is about 60 miles NW of Charlotte. Located at 2424 Century Place SE in Hickory’s primary outpatient medical corridor, the 92,516-square-foot facility was built in 2008 and expanded in 2019. The expansion added administrative offices, exam and procedure rooms, an aesthetic clinic, and improvements to the surgery center, including additional operating capacity and expanded patient areas. Founded in 1969, Graystone Eye is a physician-led ophthalmology practice serving Western North Carolina from five locations. Its team includes more than 350 employees, 14 board-certified ophthalmologists, and 5 optometrists, including 8 fellowship-trained specialists. The facility’s surgery center includes four accredited operating rooms. Flagship will provide property management and asset management services. The post Flagship Pays $51M for 92K-SF Hickory Medical Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Flagship Healthcare Properties pays $51M for 92,516-sf medical facility in Hickory, NC
100% leased Class A MOB + ASC anchored by Graystone Eye; 350+ employees, 14 ophthalmologists
Largest single-asset acquisition for Flagship Healthcare Trust; Hickory ~60 miles NW of Charlotte
stories.summary: Flagship Healthcare Properties spent $51 million acquiring a 92,516-square-foot Class A medical outpatient building and ambulatory surgery center in Hickory, North Carolina, anchored by Graystone Eye, a physician-led ophthalmology practice with 350+ employees and 14 board-certified ophthalmologists. Built in 2008 and expanded in 2019, the facility is 100% leased and represents Flagship's largest single-asset acquisition. Flagship will provide property and asset management.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; healthcare real estate REIT growth reflects robust medical services demand but does not signal residential demand drivers. Tangentially, a 350-person employer expansion or retention in Hickory (growing Charlotte secondary market) could support modest multifamily demand, but the deal is not a primary demand catalyst for apartment development.

stories.title: CMBS Conduit Capital Focuses Heavily on Multifamily, Office Sectors
stories.excerpt: The latest conduit commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) data from CRED iQ reveal a lending market that has grown more selective, not more cautious. Rates broadly eased over the past year, yet borrowers in most property types are being asked to bring more equity to the table than they were 12 months ago. Multifamily and office are the exceptions, for different reasons, and increasingly the exceptions define the cycle. Multifamily is the sector where issuers extended more credit on better terms. The loan-to-value (LTV) ratio climbed to 62 percent, up 2.2 percentage points and the highest of any property type, while the rate on those loans fell the most in the entire sample, down a full half-point to 6 percent. Debt yield actually dropped slightly, meaning borrowers are covering less cushion per dollar borrowed even as leverage rose. That is about as clean a vote of confidence as a lending market gives. Office also gained leverage, but the mechanics look different. LTV for office loans rose 3.3 points, to 49.5 percent, yet the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) fell by more than two-tenths of a turn, to 1.94 times, and debt yield ticked up rather than down. Issuers are willing to lend more against office collateral, but they’re pricing that leverage with thinner coverage and a smaller margin for error, a bet that office cash flows have stabilized enough to underwrite more aggressively, not a wholesale return of confidence in the sector. With other property sectors, trends went in a different direction, and more sharply. Retail’s LTV fell 10.2 points, to 47.8 percent, while its debt yield jumped 8.1 points, to 20.3 percent, the single largest swing in the table. Self-storage and industrial told a similar story with leverage down 6 to 10 points, respectively, while debt yield and DSCR were both up. None of these sectors is in distress, and DSCR actually improved in each case, but issuers are structuring deals that require meaningfully more sponsor equity than the
bullets: Multifamily CMBS loans hit 62% LTV (highest of all types), rates down 50 bps to 6%
Debt yield fell despite leverage increase; cleanest vote of confidence in sector lending
Office also gained leverage (LTV +3.3 pts to 49.5%) but with tighter DSCR and higher rates
stories.summary: CRED iQ's latest CMBS conduit data show a lending market that is selective rather than cautious. Multifamily borrowers secured the highest LTVs of any property type (62%, up 2.2 pts) with the lowest rates (6%, down 50 bps), while debt yield fell—signaling strong lender confidence and more credit extension on better terms. Office gained leverage (LTV 49.5%, +3.3 pts) but faced tighter debt-service coverage ratios (1.94x, -0.2 turn) and higher debt yields, reflecting more defensive underwriting.
stories.impact: Surging multifamily credit availability and improving terms (high LTV, low rates, lower cushion requirements) unlocks refinancing and acquisition capital for developers; reduces cost of capital for stabilized and pipeline assets. Conversely, office's tightening DSCR and rising debt yield signal capital flight from office to multifamily, compressing office redevelopment optionality and potentially limiting conversion-to-residential financing in core markets.

stories.title: Commercial Real Estate Investment’s Curious Rise Amid Higher Inflation, Rates
stories.excerpt: Last week, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter point while signaling another hike later this year. It seems like just yesterday that everyone in commercial real estate was bemoaning high interest rates, delaying big investments and transaction activity until the Fed saw fit to lower its benchmark rate from the 5.25 to 5.5 percent peak it had reached in 2023. To the relief of many, those rates have come down a bit, hitting a recent nadir of 3.5 to 3.75 percent in December 2025, before the raise last week bumped them to 3.75 to 4 percent. Even the lower December rate, though, was still markedly higher than the rates the industry had previously adapted to for many years until 2022, and now hoped for again. And, this time, the higher rate is accompanied by stubbornly high inflation. But, even with the knowledge that this latest rate hike was likely, the mood had clearly shifted. The smaller degree of clamor on the subject of rates reflected resignation followed by adjustment, the relative quiet really the sound of an industry adapting to a changing world and new economic realities with surprisingly little fuss. Given the state of the news and the economy of late, with tariffs, the war in Iran, and stubbornly high interest and inflation rates all making instability feel more and more like the norm, commercial real estate’s investment community could have been forgiven for keeping its collective head in the sand and its investment dollars close to the vest. But that’s not what the commercial real estate investment community has been doing. Instead, CRE investment activity has been behaving more like it might be expected to in a much more stable economic and geopolitical world. A report from Avison Young noted that investment sales volume for the first half of 2026 totaled $233.6 billion, a 14.7 percent increase from the first half of 2025 and the “strongest first half of the year since 2022,” with the first-quarter total of $120 billion in volume markin
bullets: Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4% after December 2025 low of 3.5%–3.75%
CRE market mood shifted from panic to resignation; adaptation to higher structural rates
Higher inflation persists alongside elevated rates; investor sentiment stabilizing despite headwinds
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 bps, pushing the benchmark to 3.75–4%, after easing to a December 2025 low of 3.5–3.75%. Despite rates remaining well above the pre-2022 regime and inflation remaining stubbornly high, CRE market sentiment has shifted from alarm to acceptance. Industry clamor about rate hikes has quieted as market participants adapt to the new economic reality.
stories.impact: Stabilizing sentiment and rate expectations reduce downside execution risk for multifamily financing and acquisitions; developers can plan forward with greater visibility into capital costs. However, structural rates significantly above pre-pandemic levels and persistent inflation compress real returns and underwriting margin, favoring infill and value-add over greenfield development and pushing site selection toward higher-growth corridors with supply scarcity.

stories.title: New York State’s Opportunity Zones Deadline Is Fast Approaching
stories.excerpt: New York is becoming an exciting place to build, but there’s an opportunity for even more. Gov. Kathy Hochul pledged for the state to invest $25 billion toward creating 100,000 affordable homes over a five-year period that ends next year. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has committed to build 200,000 new affordable homes and preserve another 200,000 over the next decade while working with developers to meet the city’s needs for another half-million units. State and city officials have overhauled municipal zoning laws, reduced cumbersome environmental reviews, and legalized tax abatements that would allow real estate owners to complete projects more quickly while lowering their costs over the long run. But newly permanent federal Opportunity Zones could lure additional investment into less affluent census tracts that have missed out on the state’s multifamily construction boom. Now, developers are eagerly awaiting the state’s recommendations for those new zones, which are due by Sept. 28. “I believe it’s produced a lot of housing units in a lot of areas around the country where housing is in short supply,” Chris Milner, head of investment management at Cantor Fitzgerald Asset Management, told Commercial Observer. “The fact that the new legislation is making this a permanent part of the tax code is viewed as a long-term validation of the assumption.” In 2017, Congress passed legislation allowing investors to defer taxes on previously earned capital gains temporarily when they put their assets into long-term investments called Opportunity Funds, which invest in Opportunity Zones. In addition, if investors put their gains in the funds for five years, their basis on the original investment would increase to 10 percent. But, if they stuck it out for at least 10 years, they would not have to pay taxes for any capital gains that occurred from their investment. bullets: NY State Opportunity Zone recommendations due Sept. 28; permanent federal zones now available
Hochul pledges $25B for 100K affordable homes by end of 2026; Mamdani targets 400K units
Zoning overhauls, environmental review streamlining, and tax abatements accelerate development feasibility
stories.summary: New York State's permanent federal Opportunity Zones present a fresh capital-sourcing channel for development in less affluent census tracts that have lagged in multifamily construction. Governor Hochul has committed $25 billion toward 100,000 affordable units by end of 2026, and Mayor Mamdani is pursuing 200,000 new affordable homes plus 200,000 preserved units and another 500,000 total units. State and city have streamlined zoning, reduced environmental review, and restored tax abatements to lower development costs and accelerate timelines.
stories.impact: Opportunity Zone recommendations (due Sept. 28) will unlock non-traditional equity capital (carried-interest deferral, long-term gains treatment) for affordable and mixed-income multifamily in underserved NYC neighborhoods, expanding financing menu and lowering blended cost of capital. Combined with zoning liberalization and tax incentives, OZ deployment materially expands feasible site universe for multifamily development outside core Manhattan and Brooklyn, enabling supply growth in secondary and tertiary neighborhoods (e.g., Upper Manhattan, outer Bronx, eastern Queens).
